title: Generation & decoding
scopeHtml: Logits to tokens, sampling controls (temperature, top-k, top-p, min-p), search vs sampling, determinism, logprobs, penalties, hallucination, calibration, stop and length control.

notes.title: From logits to tokens
notes.html:
The pipeline for one generated token. The last transformer layer outputs a hidden vector h. The LM head (linear layer, often tied to the embedding matrix) maps it to a vector of logits, one raw score per vocabulary token (size V, e.g. 128,000). A softmax turns logits z into probabilities: p_i = exp(z_i) / Σ exp(z_j). A decoding strategy then chooses a token, appends it to the sequence, and the model runs again. Generation repeats until an end-of-sequence token, a stop sequence or the length limit.

Temperature. Divide the logits by T before softmax: p_i ∝ exp(z_i / T).

  • T → 0: the distribution collapses onto the top token (greedy).
  • T = 1: the model's raw distribution.
  • T > 1: flatter, more random, more diverse and more errors. Temperature rescales confidence, it does not add knowledge. For factual or structured tasks use low T; for brainstorming, higher.
import numpy as np
def sample(logits, temperature=1.0, rng=np.random.default_rng()):
    z = logits / max(temperature, 1e-6)
    z -= z.max()                      # numerical stability
    p = np.exp(z); p /= p.sum()
    return rng.choice(len(p), p=p)

Worked example. Logits for three tokens: [2.0, 1.0, 0.1]. At T = 1: probabilities ≈ [0.66, 0.24, 0.10]. At T = 0.5: logits become [4, 2, 0.2] → ≈ [0.86, 0.12, 0.02]. At T = 2: [1, 0.5, 0.05] → ≈ [0.50, 0.30, 0.19]. Lower T sharpens, higher T flattens.

Real life. A weighted dice: each word is a face, and the weights are how plausible the word is; temperature loads or evens out the dice.

Interview angle. Be able to write softmax with temperature and explain what happens at T → 0 and at high T.

notes.title: Sampling strategies
notes.html:
Greedy. Always take the highest-probability token. Deterministic, but tends to be repetitive and can get stuck in loops; locally best choices do not give the best sequence.

Beam search. Keep the B highest-scoring partial sequences at each step and expand all; return the best final sequence. Good where there is one correct output (translation, summarization, speech recognition). For open-ended text it produces bland, repetitive output ("the beam search curse") and costs B× compute. Rarely used for chat.

Pure sampling. Sample from the full distribution: diverse but the long tail of unlikely tokens occasionally derails the text.

Top-k. Keep only the k most likely tokens (e.g. 40), renormalize, sample. Fixed k is awkward: when the model is confident, k=40 includes junk; when it is uncertain, k=40 may cut good options.

Top-p (nucleus). Keep the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability ≥ p (e.g. 0.9), renormalize, sample. The set size adapts: tiny when confident, large when uncertain. Most popular default.

Min-p. Keep tokens whose probability ≥ min_p × p_top (e.g. 0.05 × the top probability). Scales with confidence and stays stable at high temperature.

Order of operations. Typically temperature → top-k → top-p/min-p → sample (implementation order differs between libraries; check docs). Do not combine many knobs blindly: change one at a time and evaluate.

Practical presets. Extraction, classification, code: temperature 0 to 0.3. Chat: 0.5 to 0.8, top-p 0.9 to 0.95. Creative writing: 0.8 to 1.2 with top-p/min-p to cut the tail. Some newest APIs ignore or reject sampling parameters; follow provider guidance.

Real life. Picking dinner: only from the top three options (top-k), from whatever covers 90% of your cravings (top-p), or from anything at least half as appealing as your favourite (min-p).

notes.title: Determinism and reproducibility
notes.html:
What people expect. "With temperature 0 or a fixed seed, I get identical output every time."

Reality. Not guaranteed, even for the same model and input:

  1. Floating-point non-associativity. Summation order affects the last bits; tiny differences can flip a near-tie between two tokens, and from then on the text diverges.
  2. GPU kernels and parallelism choose different reduction orders depending on load and hardware.
  3. Batching. The server batches your request with others; matrix shapes and kernels change, so numerical results change (lack of batch invariance).
  4. Model/infra changes between calls (new version, different hardware, quantization).
  5. MoE routing and speculative decoding can add variation.
  6. Seeds control the sampling randomness only, not the logits' numerical noise.

What to do.

  • Test properties, not exact strings.
  • Store outputs you must reproduce (logging, caching).
  • Use deterministic inference modes and batch-invariant kernels if you control the stack and accept lower throughput.
  • Prefer temperature 0 plus constrained formats for consistency, but expect rare variation.
  • When comparing prompts, run multiple samples and compare distributions.

Real life. Two cashiers adding up a long receipt in different orders can differ by a rounding penny, and that penny can change the change you give.

notes.title: Logprobs and calibration
notes.html:
Logprobs. The log-probability the model assigned to a token (and optionally to the top alternatives). Uses:

  • Classification without parsing: ask for a label and compare the probabilities of the label tokens; thresholding gives a confidence score and AUC-style analysis.
  • Confidence / selective answering: abstain or escalate when the top token's probability is low.
  • Debugging: see where the model hesitated or why a format broke.
  • Reranking candidates, perplexity of text, detecting memorized or machine-generated text.

Calibration. A model is calibrated if, among answers given with probability p, a fraction p are correct. Pretrained base models are often reasonably calibrated; RLHF/preference-tuned models tend to be overconfident (probabilities pushed toward 0 and 1, verbal confidence unreliable). Measure with reliability diagrams and Expected Calibration Error on a labelled set; improve with temperature scaling on a validation set, ensembles/self-consistency, or training. Never treat raw probabilities as truth without calibration.

Caveats. Probability of a token is not the probability that a claim is true; sequence probability depends on phrasing and length; some APIs do not expose logprobs.

Real life. A weather forecaster: useful only if "70% chance of rain" means rain on about 7 days out of 10.

notes.title: Repetition
notes.html:
Why loops happen. Once a phrase appears, the model finds repeating it likely (in-context copying), and under greedy or low-temperature decoding a self-reinforcing cycle forms. Long generations and weak models loop more.

Mitigations.

  • Sampling with top-p/min-p and moderate temperature.
  • Repetition penalty (divides the logit of tokens already seen), frequency penalty (subtract proportional to count), presence penalty (subtract once if present). These reduce repetition but can hurt text that legitimately repeats (code, names, structured data), so tune lightly.
  • No-repeat n-gram constraints in beam search.
  • Length limits and stop sequences.
  • Better prompts (ask for varied output), training fixes, and detecting loops at the application level (abort and retry with different parameters).

Real life. A song stuck on repeat: nudge the needle to the next track.

notes.title: Hallucination
notes.html:
Definition. Fluent, confident output that is not grounded in truth or in the provided source ("intrinsic": contradicts the source; "extrinsic": unverifiable additions).

Causes.

  • The objective rewards plausible continuation, not truth.
  • Knowledge gaps and the knowledge cutoff; rare facts are poorly learned.
  • Training and preference data that reward confident answers over "I don't know".
  • Ambiguous or false-premise prompts.
  • Long contexts and distractors; poor retrieval.
  • Sampling randomness (higher temperature increases risk).
  • Pressure to comply (sycophancy).

Mitigation, in rough order of effect.

  1. Ground in retrieved sources; instruct "answer only from the context" and require citations.
  2. Allow and reward abstention ("I don't know", ask a clarifying question).
  3. Constrain outputs (schemas, enumerations) and use tools for facts, maths and lookups.
  4. Lower randomness for factual tasks.
  5. Verify: a second pass or model checking claims against sources, self-consistency across samples, programmatic checks.
  6. Evaluate with a hallucination test set (unanswerable questions, false premises) and track the rate.
  7. UX: show sources, uncertainty, easy correction paths.

Expectation setting. Hallucination can be reduced, not eliminated. Design systems where wrong answers are detected, bounded in impact, or reviewed by humans for high-stakes uses.

Real life. A confident storyteller who fills gaps with plausible details unless you hand them the facts.

notes.title: Stop sequences and decoding design
notes.html:
Stop sequences. Strings that end generation as soon as they appear (e.g. "\n\nUser:", "</answer>"). They stop the model from continuing into the next turn or leaking template tokens. The stop string itself is usually not included in the output.

Length control. max_tokens is a hard cap. A response ending because it hit the cap is truncated, not finished: check the finish reason, and for structured outputs a truncated JSON will not parse. Ask the model for brevity in the prompt; don't rely on the cap for style.

Decoding configuration is a design decision.

  • Task type decides temperature and sampling: extraction/classification low; brainstorming high.
  • Format constraints: use schema-constrained decoding or stop sequences to guarantee shape.
  • Latency and cost: shorter outputs, lower max_tokens, streaming.
  • Safety: avoid very high temperature in user-facing deployments.
  • Reproducibility needs: log model version, parameters and prompt version with every response.

Evaluate configurations on an eval set, not by eyeballing a few samples, and record the chosen settings per feature.

Real life. Setting the oven temperature and timer for each dish, not one setting for everything.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Mechanics. Logits → (temperature) → softmax → choose a token → repeat. Temperature T rescales confidence; T → 0 is greedy. Strategies: greedy and beam search for deterministic tasks; sampling with top-k, top-p or min-p for diversity, with top-p/min-p adapting to confidence.

Determinism. Seeds and temperature 0 do not guarantee identical outputs because of floating-point non-associativity, kernels, batching and infrastructure changes. Test properties; log what you need to reproduce.

Confidence. Logprobs give token probabilities useful for classification, abstention and debugging, but tuned models are overconfident, so calibrate before using thresholds.

Failure modes. Repetition loops (fix with sampling, penalties, limits); hallucination (fix with grounding, abstention, constraints, verification and evaluation; cannot be driven to zero); truncation at max_tokens (check finish reasons).

Design checklist. Pick sampling per task, constrain formats, set stop sequences and token limits, evaluate configurations, record parameters and model versions.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Temperature divides logits; top-p truncates the tail by cumulative probability."
  • "Temperature 0 is not a determinism guarantee."
  • "Logprobs are token confidence, not truth, and preference tuning makes them overconfident."
  • "Ground, allow abstention, verify: that is the hallucination playbook."

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through exactly what happens between the final transformer layer and the next token appearing in the output.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every decoding knob lives in this pipeline. If you cannot place temperature, top-p and penalties on it, you will misuse all of them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The last hidden state of the final position is multiplied by the unembedding matrix to give one raw score (logit) per vocabulary entry. I optionally adjust those logits (penalties, bias, temperature), convert to probabilities with softmax, optionally truncate the distribution (top-k, top-p, min-p), renormalize, and then pick a token, either argmax (greedy) or a random draw. That token is appended and the loop repeats, one token per forward pass thanks to the KV cache.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
hidden state h (d_model) for last position
   -> logits z = W_unembed h          shape [V]  (V ~ 32k..256k)
   -> logit processors: bias, repetition/frequency penalties, grammar mask
   -> z / T                           temperature
   -> softmax                          p_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j)
   -> truncation: top-k / top-p / min-p, renormalize
   -> select: argmax OR sample from p
   -> append token, update KV cache, repeat until EOS / stop / max_tokens
  • Logits are unnormalized log-probabilities up to a constant. Softmax is shift-invariant, so only differences between logits matter.
  • Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel, but only the last position's logits are used for the first generated token. Decode is sequential: one new token per step, which is why generation is memory-bandwidth bound.
  • Constrained decoding (JSON schema, grammars) works at the "logit processor" stage: invalid tokens get logit -inf before softmax.
  • Order matters. In Hugging Face generate, processors such as repetition penalty run first, then temperature, then top-k/top-p/min-p warpers. Provider APIs hide the order, so treat it as "verify" per vendor.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch

def sample_next(logits: torch.Tensor, temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95):
    # logits: [V] for the last position
    if temperature == 0:
        return int(torch.argmax(logits))          # greedy, avoid dividing by 0
    probs = torch.softmax(logits / temperature, dim=-1)
    sorted_p, idx = torch.sort(probs, descending=True)
    cum = torch.cumsum(sorted_p, dim=-1)
    keep = cum - sorted_p < top_p                 # keep token that crosses the threshold
    sorted_p = sorted_p * keep
    sorted_p /= sorted_p.sum()                    # renormalize
    return int(idx[torch.multinomial(sorted_p, 1)])

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the model "chooses" a word. The model only outputs a distribution; the decoding algorithm chooses.
  • Applying top-p to logits instead of probabilities, or forgetting to renormalize after truncation.
  • Dividing by temperature 0 instead of special-casing greedy.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is decode slower per token than prefill? → Prefill is compute-bound matmul over many tokens; decode reads all weights and the KV cache to produce one token, so it is memory-bandwidth bound.
  2. Where does a JSON grammar plug in? → As a logit mask before softmax; tokens that would break the grammar get -inf.
  3. Do logits of earlier positions matter? → Not for generation (they are used in training and for prompt logprobs), only the last position feeds the sampler.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "softmax then pick a token". The senior places each knob on the pipeline, knows truncation needs renormalization, knows constraints are logit masks, and knows where the cost sits (decode is bandwidth-bound).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that apply a stop-word list or banned-token bias at the wrong stage (post-hoc string filtering instead of logit bias) get half-generated forbidden words and wasted tokens.

questions.promptHtml: What does temperature actually do mathematically, and what happens at T=0, T=1 and T much greater than 1?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you understand temperature as a reshaping of a distribution, not a "creativity dial".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Temperature divides the logits before softmax. T<1 sharpens the distribution toward the top token, T>1 flattens it toward uniform, T=1 leaves the model's own distribution unchanged. T→0 converges to argmax, and T→infinity converges to a uniform choice over the vocabulary. It does not change the ranking of tokens, only the gaps between their probabilities.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
p_i(T) = exp(z_i/T) / sum_j exp(z_j/T).

Worked example with logits [4, 2, 0]:

T probabilities
1.0 0.867, 0.117, 0.016
0.5 0.982, 0.018, 0.000 (approx)
2.0 0.665, 0.245, 0.090

(T=1: exp(4)=54.6, exp(2)=7.39, exp(0)=1, sum 62.99. T=0.5 logits become [8,4,0]: 2981, 54.6, 1, so 0.982/0.018/0.0003. T=2 logits [2,1,0]: 7.39, 2.72, 1, sum 11.1, so 0.665/0.245/0.090.)

  • Ratio of two tokens' probabilities is exp((z_i - z_j)/T), so temperature scales the log-odds linearly.
  • High T raises the mass of the long tail. With a 100k vocabulary, even 20% tail mass gets sampled every five tokens, and one off-topic token derails everything after it. That is why high T text turns to word salad.
  • "T=0" in APIs usually means "greedy", implemented as argmax, not as a literal division.
  • Low temperature lowers diversity but does not make the model more correct; a confidently wrong top token stays wrong.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import numpy as np
z = np.array([4.0, 2.0, 0.0])
for T in (0.5, 1.0, 2.0):
    p = np.exp(z / T); p /= p.sum()
    print(T, p.round(3))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying temperature controls "randomness" without noting it only matters when you sample.
  • Setting T=0 and expecting identical outputs every call (see the non-determinism question).
  • Tuning temperature to fix factual errors.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does temperature change the argmax? → No, order is preserved for any T>0.
  2. Why do reasoning models often fix temperature? → Provider-specific; some reasoning models reject or ignore custom temperature, check the docs ("verify" per model).
  3. How is T related to entropy? → Higher T raises the entropy of the output distribution monotonically.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "higher is more creative". Senior: gives the formula, explains tail-mass mechanics, notes T=0 is a special case, and ties choice of T to task (extraction low, brainstorming moderate) plus eval evidence.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team raised T to 1.2 for "variety" in support replies; the tail-token rate produced occasional language switches and invented product names until they moved to T=0.8 with min-p.

questions.promptHtml: Compare greedy decoding, beam search and sampling. When would you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know decoding is a search/sampling choice with quality trade-offs, not just "pick the best token".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Greedy takes the argmax at every step: cheap, deterministic in principle, but can miss better sequences. Beam search keeps the B highest-scoring partial sequences, approximating the max-likelihood sequence; great when there is a single correct output like translation or ASR. Sampling draws from the (truncated) distribution; it is what chat and creative generation use because maximum likelihood text is often bland and repetitive.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Greedy is locally optimal, not globally. "The best first token" may lead to a poor sentence.
  • Beam search with width B costs about B times the compute and KV memory, and scores sequences by summed log-prob (usually length-normalized, otherwise short outputs win).
  • Holtzman et al. (2019, "The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration", ICLR 2020) showed likelihood-maximizing decoding in open-ended generation produces bland, repetitive text, which motivated nucleus (top-p) sampling.
  • Mode-seeking methods suit tasks with a narrow set of correct answers; distribution-matching methods (sampling) suit tasks where many outputs are valid. | Method | Diversity | Cost | Best for | |---|---|---|---| | Greedy | none | 1x | extraction, classification, code with tests | | Beam (B=4..5) | low | ~Bx | MT, ASR, summarization with a reference | | Sampling + truncation | tunable | 1x | chat, creative, best-of-n |

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
out = model.generate(**inputs, do_sample=False, max_new_tokens=100)                       # greedy
out = model.generate(**inputs, num_beams=4, length_penalty=1.0, early_stopping=True)      # beam
out = model.generate(**inputs, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9)               # sampling

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming beam search always beats greedy. For chat models it often yields generic or looping text.
  • Ignoring length normalization.
  • Forgetting beam search is poorly supported or absent in many hosted APIs and costs extra throughput on self-hosted servers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does beam search favor short outputs? → Each token multiplies probability by <1, so log-prob sums are more negative for longer sequences; length penalty/normalization corrects it.
  2. Does greedy guarantee the same output? → Only if the numerics are the same; see the non-determinism question.
  3. How do you get diversity with beam search? → Diverse beam search, or sample then rerank.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists the three. Senior ties method to the task's answer-space and cost, cites degeneration evidence, and mentions best-of-n/self-consistency as the practical use of sampling for accuracy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A translation service moved from sampling to beam (B=4) and gained a measurable quality bump on its reference set at 3x decode memory, forcing a batch-size reduction on the same GPUs.

questions.promptHtml: Explain top-k and top-p (nucleus) sampling. Why is top-p usually preferred, and what are its failure modes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A staple. The signal is whether you understand adaptive vs fixed truncation and why it matters.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Top-k keeps the k most likely tokens and renormalizes; top-p keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability reaches p. Top-k is fixed width, so when the model is very sure it still admits k-1 junk candidates, and when the model is uncertain (many valid tokens) it cuts valid ones. Top-p adapts the candidate set size to the model's confidence. Its weakness is that at high temperature the flattened distribution makes the nucleus large and junky.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Confident step:  [0.92, 0.03, 0.01, 0.01, ...]   top-p 0.9 -> 1 token; top-k 50 -> 50 tokens
Uncertain step:  [0.06, 0.05, 0.05, 0.04, ...]   top-p 0.9 -> hundreds; top-k 50 -> only 50
  • Both only matter when sampling. With k=1 top-k is greedy.
  • Nucleus sampling is from Holtzman et al.; the pool grows and shrinks with confidence.
  • Order: temperature first, then truncation, in most frameworks (HF, vLLM). Since temperature changes the probabilities, T=1.5, top_p=0.9 keeps far more tokens than T=0.7, top_p=0.9.
  • Tuning both at once is confusing; common vendor guidance is to adjust one (verify per provider docs).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# vLLM
from vllm import SamplingParams
sp = SamplingParams(temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95, top_k=-1, max_tokens=256)  # top_k=-1 disables (verify in your vLLM version)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting top_p=0.1 and calling it "creative".
  • Combining low top_k with high top_p and not knowing which binds.
  • Believing top-p removes hallucinations; it removes low-probability tail only.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does top_p=1.0 do? → No truncation.
  2. Which one is applied first if both are set? → Implementation specific; in HF the processors run in a defined order (top-k then top-p) so the effective set is the intersection.
  3. Why does top-p degrade at high T? → Flattening inflates the tail so the cumulative threshold is only reached after many junk tokens; min-p handles this better.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE defines both. Senior explains adaptivity with a numeric example, interaction with temperature, and picks per task with an eval.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A code-completion feature with top_k=50, T=1.0 emitted rare identifiers; switching to T=0.2 plus top_p=0.95 cut compile errors in generated snippets.

questions.promptHtml: What is min-p sampling, and what problem does it solve that top-p does not?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who track current practice from people who memorized 2020 material.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Min-p keeps only tokens whose probability is at least p_base times the probability of the top token. The threshold scales with the model's confidence: when the top token has 0.9, the cutoff is high; when the top token has only 0.1, the cutoff is low. Unlike top-p, it does not let the candidate set explode when temperature flattens the distribution, so it keeps coherence at higher temperatures.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Rule: keep token i iff p_i >= p_base * max_j p_j. Example: p_base=0.1, top token 0.60, so cutoff 0.06; with top token 0.10 the cutoff is 0.01.
  • Paper: "Turning Up the Heat: Min-p Sampling for Creative and Coherent LLM Outputs" (arXiv 2407.01082, first posted July 2024 as "Min P Sampling: Balancing Creativity and Coherence at High Temperature"). It reports gains on GPQA, GSM8K and AlpacaEval creative writing at high temperature, and adoption in Hugging Face Transformers and vLLM. Independent replication has been debated, so treat the size of the gain as "verify on your own eval".
  • Typical p_base values used in practice are around 0.05 to 0.1 (community guidance, verify).
  • Tradeoff: another hyperparameter, still no guarantee of factuality.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
out = model.generate(**inputs, do_sample=True, temperature=1.0, min_p=0.05, top_p=1.0, top_k=0)
# HF Transformers: min_p supported in recent versions (verify your version)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Stacking min-p with aggressive top-p and not knowing which one truncates.
  • Assuming hosted APIs expose min-p (many do not).
  • Copying someone's p_base without evals on your task.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the threshold scale with the max prob? → It is a relative confidence test, so it adapts like top-p but without depending on the tail mass.
  2. When is it irrelevant? → Greedy/T=0 and hosted APIs without the parameter.
  3. How would you validate it? → A/B with fixed prompts, N samples each, task metric plus diversity metric (distinct-n, self-BLEU) and human or LLM-judge preference.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "another sampling method". Senior: states the formula, why relative thresholds beat cumulative ones at high T, and insists on measuring.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A roleplay product raised T for variety and saw derailments; moving to min-p kept variety without the off-topic tokens.

questions.contextHtml:
A teammate wrote a custom sampler for a self-hosted 7B model and says "it works at T=0.7 but at T=0 the service crashes with NaN and at T=1.5 the answers are strangely good". Code:

import torch

def sample(logits, temperature, top_p):
    probs = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1)
    sorted_p, idx = torch.sort(probs, descending=True)
    cum = torch.cumsum(sorted_p, dim=-1)
    sorted_p[cum > top_p] = 0.0
    sorted_p = sorted_p / sorted_p.sum()
    scaled = torch.softmax(torch.log(sorted_p + 1e-9) / temperature, dim=-1)
    return idx[torch.multinomial(scaled, 1)]

Logs: RuntimeError: probability tensor contains either inf, nan or element < 0 at temperature=0. Eval at top_p=0.9: first token is sometimes empty-set trouble when the top token has p=0.93.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a check for T=0." That fixes one crash and misses that temperature is applied after truncation and that the cumulative mask can remove every token.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are logits float16 (softmax precision)? Is this batch-1? Is T=0 meant to be greedy? Why is there a log(x+1e-9)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Route T=0 to argmax and ship; it is a one-line guard.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) division by zero at T=0 produces inf/NaN. (b) cum > top_p masks the token that crosses the threshold, and if the top token alone exceeds top_p (0.93 > 0.9) everything is masked, leaving sum 0 and NaN after division. (c) temperature is applied after truncation, so the nucleus was selected on the T=1 distribution, which is why "T=1.5 looks good": temperature never widened the candidate set, it only reweighted survivors, an accidental top-p-then-temperature order. (d) the epsilon hack distorts tiny probabilities and zeroed tokens get revived by 1e-9 (log(0+1e-9) is finite, so masked tokens come back with nonzero probability!).
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit test with a toy distribution [0.93, 0.05, 0.02] at top_p 0.9; assert the sampled set equals {first token}. Test T=0; test that masked tokens never get sampled over 10k draws via a counter.
  5. Root cause: Wrong mask condition (must keep the token that crosses the threshold), temperature in the wrong place, and the epsilon revival of masked tokens.
  6. Fix: Use the corrected version from Q163: temperature first, keep = cum - sorted_p < top_p, renormalize, argmax for T=0.
  7. Prevention: Property tests (never sample outside the nucleus; distribution sums to 1; T→0 equals greedy), and prefer the library implementation over custom samplers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just clamp T to 1e-6, which leaves overflow risks in fp16 and still hides the ordering bug.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the model is in fp16 at T=0.1? → Logits/T may overflow; compute softmax in float32.
  • Does applying top-p before temperature ever make sense? → Rarely; it makes temperature a reweighting of a fixed set, which some people use deliberately, but it should be a conscious choice.
  • How would you test sampling statistically? → Chi-square on empirical frequency vs expected over many draws.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A custom sampler was copied across services; one copy kept the crossing-token bug, so confident steps sometimes returned an empty candidate set and the fallback was token id 0. The symptom was random "!" characters in 0.1% of replies.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only fixes the T=0 crash.
  • Hire: finds the mask bug and ordering, writes a fix.
  • Strong hire: also spots the epsilon revival, proposes property tests, and recommends using the library sampler.

questions.promptHtml: You set temperature to 0 and the model still returns different outputs on identical requests. Why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Very common senior question. It reveals whether you understand floating point, batching and serving, versus saying "randomness".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Temperature 0 removes sampling randomness, but logits are still floating-point numbers computed on GPUs. Floating-point addition is not associative, and the order of reductions in matmul, attention and normalization kernels depends on batch size, tiling and parallel scheduling. On a shared server your request lands in different batches each time, so the logits differ in the last bits. When two top tokens are near-tied, argmax flips, and after one flipped token everything downstream diverges. Mixture-of-experts routing, hardware differences and model/version rollouts add more variance.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Floating point: (a+b)+c can differ from a+(b+c) in finite precision, more so in bf16/fp16.
  • The widely discussed analysis from Thinking Machines ("Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference", Horace He et al., Sep 2025) argues the main culprit is lack of batch invariance: a given kernel is run-to-run deterministic for the same shapes, but the result for your request depends on how many other requests are batched with it, which depends on server load. Their fix was batch-invariant RMSNorm, matmul and attention kernels, at a throughput cost (figures vary by source; verify in the original post).
  • Other sources: atomics in some CUDA ops, MoE expert capacity/routing with batch composition, different GPU types or driver/kernel versions between replicas, speculative decoding acceptance details, and silent model updates behind a floating alias.
  • Near-ties matter: if the top-2 logit gap is 1e-4 (common on high entropy steps), tiny noise flips argmax. Divergence compounds because later tokens condition on the flipped one.
same prompt -> batch A (size 8) -> kernel tiling X -> logits L1
same prompt -> batch B (size 31) -> kernel tiling Y -> logits L2 (L1 != L2 in low bits)
argmax(L1) != argmax(L2) only when top-2 are near-tied

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch
a = torch.randn(10_000, dtype=torch.float32)
print(a.sum() == a.flip(0).sum())     # often False: summation order changes the result

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Answering "the model is stochastic" (at T=0 the sampler is not).
  • Blaming only "GPU concurrency" (partial and, per the post above, not the main cause).
  • Promising determinism by setting a seed (the seed controls the sampler, not kernel numerics).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What would make a self-hosted server deterministic? → Fixed batch size or batch-invariant kernels, deterministic algorithms flags, same hardware/software stack; costs throughput.
  2. Does it matter for quality? → Rarely per sample, but it breaks exact-match regression tests and caching assumptions, and affects on-policy RL.
  3. How to reduce the impact without kernel work? → Make outputs robust (structured output, short answers, logprob thresholds) and test with tolerance rather than string equality.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE says floating point and GPUs. Senior adds batch-variance as the mechanism, near-tie amplification, MoE and version drift, and states what is practical (tolerant evals, caching) vs expensive (batch-invariant kernels).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Nightly regression tests with exact string match flaked 3-5% of cases at T=0; they moved to semantic/field-level comparison and logged model version per call.

questions.contextHtml: You own two features on one self-hosted 8B model served with vLLM-style batching on 4 GPUs: (A) English-to-German product description translation, 2M items/day, reference translations exist, BLEU/COMET tracked; (B) a customer chat assistant, 40 QPS peak, p95 target 3 s. A colleague proposes "beam search with 5 beams everywhere because it finds higher-probability outputs". Current greedy decode uses ~14 GB of KV cache per GPU at the peak batch.
questions.promptHtml: Do you adopt beam search for A, B, both or neither? Defend with mechanics and cost.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Higher probability means better quality, so beam everywhere", or "beam is outdated, never use it". Both ignore task structure and cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there one correct output (A yes, B no)? Is quality measured against references? What headroom do we have in KV memory and GPU count? Is the latency target hard?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is a design decision. I would not change production before an offline test.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: For A, beam (4 to 5) likely adds a few COMET/BLEU points because the task is mode-seeking. For B, beam likely yields generic, repetitive, over-safe replies (the degeneration result of Holtzman et al.), and costs B-times KV memory.
  4. How I'd verify each: Offline on 5k held-out items for A: greedy vs beams 2/4/5 with length penalty tuned, COMET and BLEU, plus tokens/s. For B: sampled replies at T=0.7 + top-p 0.95 vs beam, human or LLM-judge preference, distinct-n, repetition rate.
  5. Root cause (of the disagreement): Beam maximizes sequence likelihood; for open-ended chat likelihood is not the goal.
  6. Fix: Beam (B=4) for A in an offline batch queue where latency is irrelevant, with throughput-optimized batching; sampling with truncation for B. Budget: beam B=4 multiplies decode KV roughly 4x, so I would cut the max batch from N to about N/4 or add GPUs.
  7. Prevention: Make decoding config part of the per-feature config, versioned, with the offline eval in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not beam for B. Not a single global decoding config. Not 'more beams = better': past B around 5 quality can drop because of the beam search curse, and the memory bill is linear.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if A must be real-time? → Use greedy or B=2, or speculative decoding to buy back latency, and measure the quality loss.
  • What if the translation outputs must be diverse for A/B testing? → Sample N and rerank.
  • How does length penalty enter? → Sum log-prob divided by length^alpha; without it, beams prefer short outputs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team enabled beam search on an assistant after a offline BLEU-like win; user surveys dropped because replies became terse and repetitive. The offline metric measured similarity to references, not helpfulness.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks one method for everything.
  • Hire: splits by task and cites the cost.
  • Strong hire: quantifies KV/batch impact, proposes the offline eval design, mentions length normalization and rerank alternatives.

questions.promptHtml: What does setting a seed do for LLM generation, and what does it not guarantee? How would you design for reproducible outputs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes whether you separate sampler randomness from numerical non-determinism and know provider limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A seed initializes the random number generator that drives the sampling step (the multinomial draw). With the same seed, same weights, same prompt, same params and identical logits, the same tokens come out. It does not fix numerical variation in logits from batching, hardware or backend changes. Providers that expose seed describe it as best-effort; OpenAI's docs say outputs are "mostly" consistent and expose system_fingerprint to detect backend changes (verify current status, as the field has been de-emphasized). For real reproducibility I log the full request, the seed, the model snapshot ID and the fingerprint, and cache responses instead of promising regeneration.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Layers of randomness: (1) sampler RNG, controlled by seed; (2) numerical kernel variance, not controlled by seed; (3) backend drift: new weights, quantization, kernels, routing changes.
  • Per-request seeds in batched servers: the engine needs a per-request RNG generator, otherwise one request's draws depend on its neighbors. vLLM exposes seed in SamplingParams for this; in HF use torch.manual_seed or pass a torch.Generator (verify the generate API in your version).
  • Microsoft's Azure OpenAI docs note larger max_tokens tends to reduce reproducibility (more steps, more chances for a near-tie flip).
  • Anthropic's Messages API has no seed parameter as of my knowledge (verify).
  • Pinned snapshot names (dated model IDs) beat floating aliases.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()
r = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-2024-08-06", seed=1234, temperature=0.7,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Name 3 fruits."}],
)
print(r.system_fingerprint, r.choices[0].message.content)  # log both

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming seed + temperature 0 gives bit-exact outputs across days.
  • Setting seed but changing any other parameter (even max_tokens) between runs.
  • Not recording the model snapshot.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you reproduce a customer-reported bad answer? → Replay the logged request with the same snapshot and seed; if it differs, check the fingerprint, then rely on the logged output as evidence.
  2. Why does a per-request seed matter in batched serving? → Shared RNG state makes results depend on batch order.
  3. Best way to give users stable answers? → Cache by hash of (prompt, params, model snapshot).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "set the seed". Senior: layers the sources of variance, designs logging and caching, pins snapshots, and writes tests tolerant of variation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An audit feature promised regenerable explanations; the provider rolled the alias model and regenerated text differed. They switched to storing generated text with its metadata.

questions.contextHtml: Your CI runs 400 LLM regression prompts nightly against a hosted API with temperature=0, seed=42. For three weeks the suite was 99.5% stable. Tuesday: 38 of 400 cases fail (9.5%), mostly exact-match on JSON field text. Logs: the response system_fingerprint changed from fp_a1b2 to fp_c3d4 at 02:10 UTC; median latency dropped 18%. No code deploy. The prompt template is unchanged; one dependency (tokenizer-based truncation helper) was bumped Monday. A PM wants the tests "fixed by tomorrow".
questions.promptHtml: What happened and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase temperature handling or retry until it passes." Retrying hides a real behavior change; blaming the seed shows a misunderstanding of what the seed controls.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the model ID a dated snapshot or alias? Do failures cluster by prompt length or type? Did the helper bump change the truncated prompt? Are the diffs semantic or only whitespace/wording?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not mute tests. Mark the run as "backend changed" and run the 38 failures twice more to measure flakiness; keep a baseline of old outputs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) provider backend change (the fingerprint flip is a strong hint, plus faster latency suggests different kernels, quantization or hardware). (b) Monday's helper changed prompt bytes for long inputs. (c) Alias moved to a new snapshot. (d) exact-match assertions are fragile to near-tie token flips.
  4. How I'd verify each: Diff the actual prompts sent (hash prompt bytes before and after the bump) to rule out (b); check whether failures correlate with fingerprint using logged data; replay failing prompts and request logprobs to see top-2 gaps at the divergence token (small gaps mean a near-tie; large gaps mean a real behavior shift); run the same prompts on the pinned older snapshot.
  5. Root cause: In my scenario: prompt hashes identical, failures only on the new fingerprint, divergence tokens with small logprob gaps. The backend changed numerics, flipping near-ties; and the assertions were stricter than the task needs.
  6. Fix: Short term: re-baseline with the new fingerprint after a human spot check of the 38 diffs. Long term: replace exact match with field-level and semantic checks (schema validity, enum equality, normalized string similarity, LLM judge only for free text), and run each case N=3 with majority/threshold rules.
  7. Prevention: Log model ID, fingerprint, prompt hash per call; alert on fingerprint change; pin dated snapshots; separate "determinism" canaries (a small set expected stable) from quality evals.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not auto-retry until green. Not loosening everything to a vibe check. Not pinning forever; providers deprecate snapshots, so I need a scheduled migration eval.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if logprobs aren't available? → Compare repeated runs for variance and use semantic diff; measure per-field disagreement rate.
  • What if the new output is actually better? → Then regression tests must compare against quality criteria, not the old string.
  • What if the provider denies a change? → Treat the fingerprint as evidence, keep logs, and test on a pinned snapshot.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team spent two days bisecting their own commits for a nightly failure that turned out to be a backend rollout. They then added a header-and-fingerprint dashboard that turned such incidents into a five-minute check.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retries or lowers thresholds blindly.
  • Hire: uses the fingerprint, rules out prompt change, moves to tolerant assertions.
  • Strong hire: uses logprob gaps to distinguish near-tie noise from behavior shift, and designs canaries and monitoring.

questions.promptHtml: What are token logprobs, and what practical uses do they have in an LLM application?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Logprobs are an underused signal. Senior candidates know when they are trustworthy and when they are not.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A logprob is the log of the probability the model assigned to a token. APIs can return it for the chosen token and the top-N alternatives. Uses: confidence scoring (e.g. gating low-confidence answers to a human), classification (read the probabilities of the label tokens instead of parsing text), threshold-based routing, detecting where a generation went off, perplexity/eval of fixed text, and debugging near-tie non-determinism. Caveat: they reflect the model's token-level belief, which is not guaranteed to be calibrated, especially after RLHF.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Probability = exp(logprob). Logprob -0.01 means about 99%, -2.3 means 10%.
  • Sequence confidence: sum (joint probability) or mean logprob (length-normalized). Joint probability shrinks with length, so compare like with like.
  • For classification: constrain output to one token per label (e.g. "A"/"B"), set max_tokens=1, request top logprobs, and normalize over the label tokens only: p_label = exp(lp_label) / sum exp(lp_labels). Careful with tokenization variants such as " yes" vs "yes".
  • Availability: OpenAI chat completions return logprobs with top_logprobs (up to 20, verify); vLLM and HF give them; Anthropic's Messages API does not expose token logprobs (verify). Some reasoning models do not return them (verify).
  • Calibration: pretrained models are often well calibrated; instruction-tuned / RL models tend to be overconfident (OpenAI GPT-4 report discusses calibration degrading after post-training; verify).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import math
r = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini", max_tokens=1, logprobs=True, top_logprobs=5, temperature=0,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Is this review positive? Answer Y or N.\n\nGreat battery."}],
)
top = r.choices[0].logprobs.content[0].top_logprobs
probs = {t.token: math.exp(t.logprob) for t in top}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating raw token probability as "probability the answer is correct".
  • Not normalizing over label tokens or ignoring case/space variants.
  • Averaging logprobs over a long answer and using one global threshold.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you pick the confidence threshold? → Plot reliability on a labeled set, choose by precision/coverage trade-off.
  2. Why is the first token's logprob often misleading? → It may be a format token ("The", "{") with high confidence, while the key content token is later; look at the content tokens.
  3. How do you handle APIs without logprobs? → Self-consistency across N samples, or verbalized confidence calibrated on a labeled set.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "confidence score". Senior: explains normalization, tokenization pitfalls, calibration, and validates thresholds on labeled data.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A triage classifier read the label token logprobs and sent anything under 0.8 to humans, cutting human review volume by a large fraction at the same error rate, verified on a labeled week.

questions.contextHtml: A support pipeline classifies 3M tickets/month into 12 intents using a large model with a 600-token prompt and a free-text JSON answer; avg output 45 tokens. Pricing assumption (illustrative): $3 per 1M input, $12 per 1M output. Monthly cost: input 3M x 600 = 1.8B tokens = $5,400; output 3M x 45 = 135M tokens = $1,620; total $7,020. Accuracy 91%. The business wants cost cut 60% without dropping below 90%. You find the provider returns top-20 logprobs.
questions.promptHtml: How do you cut the cost and keep accuracy? What can go wrong?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to a smaller model" with no evaluation plan, or "just shorten the prompt" without noticing output tokens and routing opportunities.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the confusion matrix skewed? Are labels fixed? What does a wrong label cost vs human review? Latency target? Are logprobs supported on the small model?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is optimization. Start by measuring.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Output tokens can drop from 45 to 1 by labeling intents with single-token codes (A..L) and reading logprobs. (b) A small model plus logprob thresholding handles most tickets; escalate uncertain ones to the large model. (c) Prompt caching of the static instruction prefix reduces the input bill (provider-dependent, verify discounts).
  4. How I'd verify each: On 5k labeled tickets: small model with single-token output; compute max normalized label prob; plot accuracy vs coverage; pick threshold t where small-model accuracy above t is >= 95%. Compute the share handled.
  5. Root cause (of the cost): Most spend is input tokens from a long prompt on a large model plus verbose output.
  6. Fix: Cascade: small model, max_tokens=1, top_logprobs; if p_top >= t (say 0.9) accept; else call the large model. Illustrative numbers: if the small model costs 1/10 the price and handles 75% at threshold, cost ~ 0.1 x 7,020 + 0.25 x 7,020 x (output now tiny) approx $700 + ~$1,500 = about $2,200 (about 69% savings) before caching; I would verify on real traffic.
  7. Prevention: Monitor accept rate and a weekly audit sample of accepted items; recalibrate when prompts or traffic shift; alarm on drift in mean max-prob.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not trust the threshold from one week; not remove the escalation path; not ignore label-token tokenization (the letter " A" vs "A"). Single-letter codes lose some semantic help versus label names, so test names with distinct first tokens too.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the small model is overconfident on a rare intent? → Per-class thresholds or calibration (temperature scaling on logits is not available via API; use isotonic/Platt on the returned probs).
  • What if logprobs are unavailable? → Use N=3 sampled agreement or fine-tune a small classifier on the large model's labels.
  • What if traffic distribution shifts? → The threshold's precision changes; monitor audited accuracy per segment.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cascade saved most of the bill until a product launch introduced a new ticket type; the small model confidently misrouted it at p~0.95. A weekly audit of accepted samples caught it in days.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swaps models only.
  • Hire: single-token output plus logprob routing with a labeled threshold.
  • Strong hire: computes the cost, calibration per class, audit loop, and a fallback when logprobs are absent.

questions.promptHtml: Explain repetition, frequency and presence penalties. How do they differ, and what do they break?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of logit-processor math and the side effects in structured or factual outputs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: They all lower the logits of tokens that already appeared, to fight loops. The OpenAI-style frequency penalty subtracts a value proportional to how many times a token has appeared; the presence penalty subtracts a flat value once a token has appeared at all. The Hugging Face repetition_penalty (from the CTRL paper) is multiplicative: it divides positive logits and multiplies negative logits by the penalty for seen tokens. All are blunt: they penalize legitimate repeats like JSON keys, names, code identifiers and numbers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• OpenAI documented form: logit_j -> logit_j - c_j * frequency_penalty - 1[c_j > 0] * presence_penalty, where c_j is the count of token j in the output so far (documented range -2 to 2; verify). Positive values discourage repetition; negative ones encourage it.
  • HF/CTRL: for seen tokens, logit = logit / theta if logit > 0 else logit * theta, theta=1.0 means off; typical values 1.05 to 1.3 (verify). It applies to prompt and generated tokens in HF, which can suppress words copied from the input.
  • no_repeat_ngram_size in HF forbids repeating any n-gram, a hard ban, and breaks things like repeated phrases or names.
  • Why loops happen at all: once a phrase repeats, the model's induction-like copying makes the next repeat more likely (self-reinforcing), especially under greedy/low temperature. | Penalty | Scales with count | Affects | |---|---|---| | frequency | yes | proportional discouragement | | presence | no | one-time "topic diversity" nudge | | repetition (HF) | no, multiplicative | prompt+output tokens |

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
out = model.generate(**inputs, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7,
                     repetition_penalty=1.1, no_repeat_ngram_size=0)  # tune, don't assume

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Applying penalties to JSON/code generation: keys and braces repeat legitimately.
  • Using large values (e.g. 2.0) and getting broken grammar or odd synonyms.
  • Using penalties to cover for a prompt/stop-condition bug.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the multiplicative form treat negative logits differently? → Dividing a negative logit would raise it, the wrong direction.
  2. Which would you use to encourage topic diversity in brainstorming? → Mild presence penalty.
  3. Better alternatives for loops? → Slightly higher temperature, min-p/top-p, DRY-style n-gram samplers (community feature in some servers; verify), fixing the prompt, or a better model.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "reduces repetition". Senior: writes both formulas, knows the HF prompt-token effect, warns about structured outputs, and treats penalties as a last resort.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team enabled frequency_penalty=1.0 globally; extraction output lost repeated field names and numbers, dropping JSON validity until penalties were set to 0 for structured calls.

questions.contextHtml: A self-hosted 13B summarizer (vLLM, greedy, T=0, max_tokens=4096) starts producing runaway outputs. Overnight: 0.8% of requests (about 2,400/day of 300k) hit max_tokens with a looping phrase, e.g. ...the committee approved the plan. The committee approved the plan. The committee approved the plan.... Those requests hold decode slots 40x longer than average (4096 vs ~100 tokens), p95 latency rose from 4 s to 19 s and GPU cost is up 22%. Changes this week: a new document source with long meeting transcripts (avg 28k tokens, context limit 32k), and a quantization update (fp16 to int8) rolled Thursday. Loop rate was 0.05% before.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix without a model retrain.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set repetition_penalty to 1.5." It might reduce loops but damages summaries and ignores the real triggers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do loops correlate with input length, source, or the quantized replicas? Is the loop at the start or after a long coherent piece? Did the prompt template change for the new source?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap max_tokens by task (a summary rarely needs more than 600) and add a loop detector (stop if the last 50 tokens repeat an earlier 50-token window) that aborts and retries with sampling. This restores slot capacity fast.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Long inputs near the context limit (28k of 32k) push the model into degenerate copying; truncation or lost instructions at the end. (b) Greedy decoding is vulnerable to loops by nature. (c) int8 quantization perturbs logits and pushes borderline cases into loops. (d) prompt template places the instruction at the start of a very long context so it is under-attended.
  4. How I'd verify each: Bucket loop rate by input length and by replica quantization (A/B the fp16 vs int8 on the same 2k failing prompts); inspect logprobs of the loop tokens (loops usually have rising probabilities, e.g. >0.95 per token); test sampling T=0.3 + min-p vs greedy on the failing set.
  5. Root cause: In my scenario: loops concentrated in inputs >25k tokens and 3x more frequent on int8 replicas. Greedy plus long context plus slightly noisier logits made self-reinforcing repetition likely.
  6. Fix: Short term: max_tokens cap, loop detector with retry at T=0.3, min_p=0.05; chunk-and-merge (map-reduce) summarization for inputs over about 16k; restore fp16 on the long-input route. Long term: evaluate the int8 quantization on a long-document suite before rollout; move instructions to the end of the prompt too.
  7. Prevention: Metric: fraction of responses hitting max_tokens, by route; canary evals on long docs for any quantization change; alert at 0.2%.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a global repetition_penalty (hurts names and numbers in summaries). Not raising max_tokens. Not retrying greedy (same loop again).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if loops start mid-output at a stable 800 tokens? → Possible KV cache/position issue; test with a different context window and engine version.
  • Would a stop sequence help? → Not for unknown loop text; a detector is generic.
  • Can speculative decoding make loops worse? → It does not change the target distribution, so no, but check the implementation for acceptance bugs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A looping minority of requests consumed a third of a cluster's decode time because each ran to the max. Capping output length per route paid for itself the same day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: just adds a penalty.
  • Hire: caps length, adds a detector, correlates with length and quantization.
  • Strong hire: uses logprobs and A/B on failing prompts, proposes map-reduce for long inputs, and sets rollout gates and metrics.

questions.promptHtml: Explain batch invariance and why it, rather than "GPU randomness", is the crux of LLM inference non-determinism. What would it cost to fix?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A deep-dive follow-up to the T=0 question. It separates people who read the recent literature and think in kernels from those who repeat folklore.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A kernel is batch-invariant if the result for one request does not depend on what else is in the batch. Most GPU kernels are run-to-run deterministic for a fixed input shape, but inference servers change the effective shape per request as load changes the batch size, and kernels pick different reduction orders or split strategies for different shapes. Since floating-point addition is not associative, the logits differ in low bits, and near-tied argmax flips. Fixing it means batch-invariant RMSNorm, matmul and attention kernels with a fixed reduction order, which costs throughput, so it is a choice, not a free flag.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Source: Thinking Machines, "Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference" (Sep 2025). They identify RMSNorm, matmul and attention as the places where reduction strategy varies with batch size, and ship batch-invariant replacements plus a vLLM demonstration. Reported overhead figures differ between summaries; read the post for numbers before quoting any.
  • Mechanism for matmul: for small batches the kernel may split the K dimension across more cores (split-K) to use the GPU; for large batches it uses different tiling. Different splits mean different summation orders.
  • Attention: split-KV strategies for decode depend on the number of sequences and KV length; prefix caching and chunked prefill change which tokens are processed in which kernel call, making outputs depend on cache state.
  • Design principle: pick one reduction order independent of batch size and sequence-split, accepting lower peak utilization.
  • Why it matters beyond tests: in RL post-training, mismatch between the sampler's numerics and the trainer's numerics makes "on-policy" data subtly off-policy; bitwise-equal inference removes that mismatch (the post makes this argument).
  • Even with invariant kernels you still need: same hardware/driver stack, deterministic MoE routing, and fixed model snapshot.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import torch
torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)   # forces deterministic variants where available
# note: this addresses run-to-run determinism for fixed shapes,
# not batch invariance of your serving engine's kernels

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating "deterministic" with "batch-invariant". Setting deterministic flags does not make a request's output independent of its neighbors.
  • Quoting a specific slowdown percentage without citing the version and workload.
  • Believing hosted APIs can offer it cheaply; it is a throughput trade for the provider.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does atomics-based "concurrency" not explain most of it? → Common forward-pass kernels avoid atomics and are deterministic for fixed shapes; the variance comes from shape-dependent strategies.
  2. How would you test batch invariance? → Run the same prompt alone and inside batches of varying sizes, compare logits bitwise at each step.
  3. When would you pay for it? → On-policy RL, audited/regulated reproducibility, high-stakes regression testing; not for typical chat.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "floating point is non-associative". Senior: names batch-variance, the three kernels, the throughput trade, and where determinism is worth paying for.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team doing RL fine-tuning saw training reward diverge from rollout reward; a train/inference numerics mismatch was part of the cause, motivating bitwise-aligned kernels.

questions.promptHtml: At a conceptual level, why do language models hallucinate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: To see whether you have a mechanistic model of hallucination, which determines which mitigation you reach for.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The model is trained to produce plausible continuations, not to verify truth. When it lacks the fact, the most plausible continuation is still a fluent, confident guess; nothing in next-token training teaches abstention. Contributing causes: knowledge gaps and rare facts seen once in training, noisy or contradictory training data, evaluations and post-training that reward guessing over saying "I don't know", sampling that occasionally picks tail tokens, exposure bias where earlier mistakes condition later text, and context problems such as missing or ignored retrieved evidence.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Kalai et al., "Why Language Models Hallucinate" (OpenAI, arXiv 2509.04664, 2025): argues hallucinations are statistical errors; pretraining cross-entropy encourages calibration, and facts with no learnable pattern (arbitrary facts seen rarely) are inherently hard, with an error rate bounded below by how often such facts appear once in the data (the "singleton rate" argument, see the paper for the exact bound). They also argue benchmarks that score "I don't know" as zero incentivize guessing, so post-training pushes toward confident answers.
  • Earlier: Kalai and Vempala, "Calibrated Language Models Must Hallucinate" (2023).
  • Taxonomy useful in interviews: | Type | Example | Typical fix | |---|---|---| | Parametric knowledge gap | wrong birth year | retrieval, tools | | Faithfulness to context | summary adds a claim | grounding prompts, citation checks | | Reasoning error | arithmetic slip | tool use, verification | | Instruction/format | invents fields | constrained decoding |
  • Decoding contributes only partly: sampling more randomly increases rate, but greedy models still hallucinate.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# Cheap detector idea: sample N answers, flag disagreement (self-consistency)
answers = [gen(q, temperature=0.8) for _ in range(5)]
confident = len(set(map(normalize, answers))) == 1

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Lower the temperature to remove hallucinations."
  • Saying the model "lies" or "knows it doesn't know" without evidence; calibration is partial.
  • Treating all hallucination as one problem.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do rare facts hallucinate more? → Little or one-time exposure, so no reliable pattern; the model interpolates plausible values.
  2. Why can post-training increase confident wrong answers? → Reward and eval schemes that don't penalize guessing more than abstaining.
  3. Is hallucination solvable? → It can be reduced and made detectable via grounding, tools, abstention training, and verification, but not guaranteed to zero for a generative model.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "model makes things up". Senior: categorizes types, ties each to a mitigation, cites the incentive/evaluation argument, and acknowledges residual risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A legal-research tool's fabricated citations were a knowledge-gap hallucination; retrieval plus citation verification against a case database fixed it, not temperature tweaks.

questions.promptHtml: Which mitigations for hallucination operate at the decoding/generation layer, and what are their limits compared with retrieval and evaluation-side fixes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers should pick the right layer for the failure and know where decoding tricks stop working.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Decoding-layer levers: lower temperature or truncation (reduces tail-token errors, not knowledge gaps), constrained decoding (guarantees structure and enumerated values, not truth), logprob thresholds to abstain or escalate, self-consistency across samples to detect unstable claims, and contrastive or verification-style decoding methods from research. They help detect or limit errors but do not add knowledge. Real fixes for knowledge gaps sit upstream: retrieval or tools for grounding, abstention training and prompts, and downstream verification (citation checks, NLI-style entailment against sources), plus measuring with a hallucination-specific eval.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layer             Lever                          Catches
prompt            "answer only from context"     faithfulness slips
retrieval/tools   ground in documents / APIs     knowledge gaps
decoding          low T, min-p, constraints      tail-token errors, format errors
confidence        logprob/self-consistency gate  unstable answers -> abstain
verification      entailment / citation check    unsupported claims
training          abstention-aware RLHF/eval     incentive to guess
  • Self-consistency (sample N, compare) detects instability, costs N times tokens; consistent-but-wrong answers survive.
  • Research decoding such as contrastive decoding / DoLa (layer-contrast) reports factuality gains in papers; effect sizes vary by model, treat as "verify on your eval".
  • Constrained decoding with enums: guarantees the value is one of N valid IDs, so a hallucinated ID is impossible but a wrong valid ID is still possible.
  • Logprob gating: use content-token logprobs (not formatting tokens) and a threshold tuned on labeled data.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def answer_or_abstain(q, ctx):
    r = llm(q, ctx, temperature=0, logprobs=True)
    content = [t.logprob for t in r.tokens if t.is_content]
    if sum(content) / len(content) < THRESH or not citations_supported(r.text, ctx):
        return "I can't verify that from the provided sources."
    return r.text

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing low temperature fixes factuality.
  • Using a logprob threshold tuned on one domain across all.
  • Constrained decoding giving false assurance about truth.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not always use self-consistency? → N-fold cost and latency, and it misses consistently wrong answers.
  2. How do you measure hallucination rate? → Labeled set with claim-level support checks, human review sample, LLM judge validated against humans.
  3. When is abstention the right default? → When the cost of a wrong answer exceeds the cost of a miss; tune per domain.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE lists techniques. Senior maps technique to failure type and layer, states what each cannot do, and ties to a measured abstain/escalate policy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A healthcare FAQ bot reduced unsupported answers mainly by retrieval and citation verification; the logprob gate caught the remainder at a cost of more escalations.

questions.promptHtml: What is calibration for an LLM, how would you measure it, and why does it matter for decoding-time decisions?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Using confidence signals safely depends on calibration; senior candidates know it is not free and can drift with training.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A model is calibrated if its stated confidence matches observed accuracy: of answers given at 80% confidence, about 80% are right. I measure it on labeled data with a reliability diagram and Expected Calibration Error (ECE), binning predictions by confidence and comparing average confidence to accuracy in each bin. Base pretrained models are often reasonably calibrated; instruction tuning and RL tend to make them overconfident, so I recalibrate (e.g. Platt scaling or isotonic regression on logprob-derived scores) before using any threshold for abstention or routing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• ECE = sum over bins b of (n_b / N) * |acc(b) - conf(b)|. Example: 3 bins, 40% of items at conf 0.9 with acc 0.7, 40% at 0.6 with acc 0.55, 20% at 0.3 with acc 0.35: ECE = 0.4x0.2 + 0.4x0.05 + 0.2x0.05 = 0.11.
  • Confidence sources: token/answer-level probability (needs logprobs; for multi-token answers normalize across label options), self-consistency agreement, verbalized confidence ("I'm 80% sure", usually poorly calibrated), or a trained verifier.
  • Evidence: the GPT-4 technical report shows a calibration plot where the pretrained model is well calibrated and the post-trained one less so (verify the exact figure); Kalai et al. (2025) relate this to objectives that do not reward calibration. Temperature scaling of the final softmax is a classic recalibration method for classifiers when you have logits (self-hosted only).
  • Calibration is domain-specific and shifts with prompt wording, so recalibrate when the prompt or distribution changes.
  • ECE alone can hide issues (it ignores resolution); also report accuracy-vs-coverage curves and Brier score.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import numpy as np
def ece(conf, correct, bins=10):
    conf, correct = np.asarray(conf), np.asarray(correct)
    edges = np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)
    total = 0.0
    for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
        m = (conf > lo) & (conf <= hi)
        if m.any():
            total += m.mean() * abs(correct[m].mean() - conf[m].mean())
    return total

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using verbalized confidence as if calibrated.
  • Evaluating calibration on too few items per bin.
  • Forgetting that temperature at inference changes the confidence values you read back.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you recalibrate an API model without logits? → Fit isotonic/Platt on returned probabilities or agreement scores using a labeled set.
  2. Does a well-calibrated model hallucinate less? → It knows when it is unsure only on average; per-instance reliability still varies, and hallucination of arbitrary facts persists.
  3. Accuracy-coverage vs ECE? → For abstention policies the accuracy-coverage curve is what directly informs the threshold.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "calibration means probabilities are accurate". Senior: computes ECE, knows post-training degrades it, recalibrates per domain, and uses the curve to set thresholds.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A routing cascade's threshold from a pretrained-model blog post sent too many wrong answers through on the tuned model; recalibrating on 3k labeled in-domain items fixed the accept precision.

questions.contextHtml: A pipeline extracts structured records using a few-shot prompt where each example ends with ###. Config: stop=["###"], max_tokens=300, T=0. After a prompt refactor, 6% of requests (about 18k/day of 300k) return truncated JSON: {"name": "Acme", "items": [{"sku": "A1", "qty": 2}, {"sku": "A2", "q with finish_reason: "length". Another 1.5% return output containing a premature cut: {"note": "Use ### for headers" ending at the first ### inside a field value, finish_reason: "stop". Average output was 140 tokens before; orders with 20+ line items now average 380. Parsing errors page the on-call; retries cost 7% more tokens.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose both failure modes and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise max_tokens to 4000 and use a different stop string." Raising limits blindly increases cost and latency, and misses that stop sequences match anywhere in generated text.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in the refactor (new fields, longer examples)? Which requests truncate (line item count)? Is finish_reason logged? Does the API support structured outputs / JSON schema?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise max_tokens only for the route that needs it (to 1,000 for large orders, based on a p99 of 380 plus margin) and treat finish_reason == "length" as a failure that triggers a continuation or a chunked retry, not as parseable output.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The refactor added fields so outputs for large orders exceed 300 tokens (length truncation; check the log excerpt, finish_reason: length). (b) The ### stop matches inside content, causing premature stop. (c) Stop sequence tokenization: stops are matched on text, but the provider may hold back partial matches; usually fine, but the stop string itself is not returned. (d) Red herring: T=0 or non-determinism is not the cause, since failures correlate with item count.
  4. How I'd verify each: Bucket truncation rate by number of input items; count tokens of failed outputs with the model's tokenizer (e.g. tiktoken) to see that they cluster at exactly 300; grep outputs for the stop string in field values; check finish_reason distribution.
  5. Root cause: Output length distribution grew past the cap, and the delimiter used for few-shot formatting is a plausible string in user data.
  6. Fix: Short term: dynamic max_tokens from the input item count; treat length finish as error; change the stop to a delimiter that cannot occur in data (or none). Long term: use schema-constrained structured outputs or JSON mode so the model emits a closed JSON object and stops on its own at EOS, with prefilled structure; split large orders into batches of 10 items.
  7. Prevention: Log finish_reason and output token counts with p50/p99 alerts; a test with adversarial data containing the delimiter; a lint rule that stop strings are unique tokens like <|end|> not in the input.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a huge global max_tokens (cost, latency, and runaway output). Not parsing partial JSON with regex repair as the main strategy. Constrained decoding adds first-request grammar compile overhead and may not fit every schema feature; verify the supported subset.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if max_tokens includes reasoning tokens in a reasoning model? → Budget is shared, so visible output can be cut; set a larger completion budget (verify the parameter name and semantics for the model).
  • What if the stop string spans two tokens? → Providers match on decoded text; self-hosted engines also do, but verify in vLLM that stop uses string matching and include_stop_str_in_output defaults (verify).
  • How do you stream with stop sequences? → The engine must hold back the last few characters to avoid emitting a partial stop string, adding slight latency.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "###" delimiter worked for months until a customer pasted markdown into a notes field; a tiny share of records ended silently mid-sentence with finish_reason stop and passed validation because the JSON was still closed by a repair routine.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases limits only.
  • Hire: distinguishes the two finish reasons and fixes both causes.
  • Strong hire: adds schema-constrained outputs, token-length-based budgeting, observability, and adversarial tests.

questions.contextHtml: A product lead says: "Make the assistant more consistent but still natural." The assistant (a single hosted model, ~2M conversations/week) serves three modes: (1) policy answers from a knowledge base, (2) JSON action planning for tool calls, (3) friendly small talk. Current global config: T=0.8, top_p=1.0, no seed. Metrics: policy answer factual-consistency 88% (judge), tool-call schema validity 94%, user thumbs-up on small talk 71%. Complaint tickets: "it gave me two different refund policies on the same question", and "the bot sounds robotic" since last week's tweak that set T=0.2 for everyone in a canary (5% of traffic); in the canary schema validity rose to 97% but small-talk thumbs-up fell to 63%.
questions.promptHtml: What decoding strategy would you propose, and how do you find out if it worked?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Pick one temperature, like 0.5." That ignores that three modes have different objectives and that "consistency" is not purely a sampling issue.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "consistent" mean: same answer for same question (factual), same tone (persona), or same format? Is the refund inconsistency caused by retrieval differences? Do we log the retrieved context and parameters per call?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the global canary; revert small talk to its previous setting.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The refund inconsistency stems from different retrieved chunks or prompt versions, not temperature; (b) sampling noise at T=0.8 in policy mode adds wording variance and occasional wrong details; (c) schema validity improvements are cheap through constrained decoding rather than low temperature; (d) the small-talk drop is a lost-diversity effect (robotic, repetitive).
  4. How I'd verify each: Replay 500 logged policy questions with fixed retrieved context at T=0.8 vs T=0.2; measure answer agreement and factual consistency; compare retrieval logs for the complaint cases; test schema-constrained decoding on tool mode; A/B small talk at T=0.7 + min-p or top-p 0.95 vs 0.2 measuring thumbs-up and distinct-n.
  5. Root cause: One config applied to three objectives, plus un-pinned retrieval and prompts producing "inconsistent policy".
  6. Fix: Per-mode config: policy answers T0.0 to 0.2 with grounding and cached answers for FAQ-like questions; tool planning T=0 plus structured outputs; small talk T0.7 to 0.9 with truncation. Cache policy answers by (normalized question, KB version) so repeats are literally identical. Pin model snapshot.
  7. Prevention: Per-mode dashboards (validity, factual consistency, thumbs-up), config in versioned files, canary gates by mode, and a consistency probe (same question N times, measure agreement) in CI.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not claim T=0 gives guaranteed consistency (it does not; see the non-determinism question), hence caching. Not ship a global change evaluated on one metric. Caching may serve stale policy; key on KB version.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the model API only allows temperature in 0 to 1 and no seed? → Use T low for policy, caching for repeatability.
  • What if a user asks the same question twice and expects a fresh phrasing? → Distinguish factual consistency (stable facts) from surface variation; allow rephrasing only in small talk.
  • Cost impact? → Caching reduces calls; constrained decoding adds minor overhead; net should reduce spend.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team chased "inconsistent answers" by cutting temperature for weeks; the real cause was a retriever returning different top-3 chunks due to an index refresh. Logging retrieved doc IDs per answer ended the argument.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks one global temperature.
  • Hire: separates modes and sets parameters per mode with measurements.
  • Strong hire: clarifies the meaning of consistency, finds non-sampling causes, uses caching and constrained decoding, and defines canary metrics per mode.
